New Features in JavaScript 2023

blocks.text: New Array Features in 2023

rows: Returns the value of the last element that satisfies a condition
Returns the index of the last element that satisfies a condition

blocks.text: Browser Support
ECMAScript 2023 is supported in all modern browsers since July 2023:
JavaScript Array findLast() Method

ES2023 added the findLast() method that will start from the end of an array and return
the value of the first element that satisfies a condition.

const temp = [27, 28, 30, 40, 42, 35, 30];

let high = temp.findLast(x => x > 40);
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: JavaScript Array findLastIndex() Method
The findLastIndex() method finds the index of the last element that satisfies a condition.

const temp = [27, 28, 30, 40, 42, 35, 30];

let pos = temp.findLastIndex(x => x > 40);
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: JavaScript Array toReversed() Method
ES2023 added the Array toReversed() method as a safe way to reverse an array without altering the original array.

The difference between the new toReversed() method and the old reverse() method is that the new method
creates a new array, keeping the original array unchanged, while the old method altered the original array.

const months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr"];

const reversed = months.toReversed();
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: JavaScript Array toSorted() Method
ES2023 added the Array toSorted() method as a safe way to sort an array without altering the original array.

The difference between the new toSorted() method and the old sort() method is that the new method
creates a new array, keeping the original array unchanged, while the old method altered the original array.

const months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr"];

const sorted = months.toSorted();
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: JavaScript Array toSpliced() Method
ES2023 added the Array toSpliced() method as a safe way to splice an array without altering the original array.

The difference between the new toSpliced() method and the old splice() method is that the new method
creates a new array, keeping the original array unchanged, while the old method altered the original array.

const months = ["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr"];

const spliced = months.toSpliced(0, 1);
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: JavaScript Array with() Method
ES2023 added the Array with() method as a safe way to update elements in an array without altering the original array.

const months = ["Januar", "Februar", "Mar", "April"];

const new = months.with(2, "March");
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: #! JavaScript Shebang

In operating systems, a shebang (also known as hashbang, pound-bang, sharp-exclamation or hash-pling)
is a sequence of two characters: a number sign (#) and an exclamation mark (!).
#! at the beginning of a script tells the operating system what interpreter should be used to execute the script:
#!/usr/bin/env node
blocks.caption: Example

blocks.text: The example above tells the operating system to use the node program to run the script.

Now, you can run JavaScript code with ./fileName.js instead
of node fileName.js.
